mahabharata:12:23.7	You have full knowledge of the Veda and great austerity practised; you ought to bear the burden of the kingdom of your father and grandfather.
mahabharata:12:23.8	Austerity, sacrifice, learning, begging, restraint of the senses, meditation, solitude, contentment and giving according to ability,
mahabharata:12:23.9	these, great king, are the activities of Brahmanas that bring perfection; I shall tell of those for kshatriyas, which you also know again.
mahabharata:12:23.11	Full knowledge of the Veda, austerity well practised, acquisition of wealth and giving abundantly to worthy recipients,
mahabharata:12:23.12	these are the well-done deeds of kings, lord of men; we have heard that they accomplish this world and the next.
mahabharata:12:23.13	Of them, son of Kunti, the bearing of the rod is called the best; for strength is ever in the kshatriya and the rod rests in strength.
mahabharata:12:23.14	These are the activities of kshatriyas, king, that bring perfection; Brihaspati also sang this verse:
mahabharata:12:23.15	The earth swallows these two, as a serpent lying in its hole swallows: a king who does not resist and a Brahmana who does not travel.
mahabharata:12:23.16	And the royal sage Sudyumna too is heard to have attained supreme perfection by bearing the rod, like Daksha son of Prachetas.
[Vyasa said:] "Here too they tell this ancient history: Shankha and Likhita were two brothers of strict vows.
They each had a lovely hermitage of his own, furnished with trees bearing ever flowers and fruit, along the Bahuda river.
Then once Likhita came to Shankha's hermitage; by chance Shankha had gone out of the hermitage.
Coming to his brother Shankha's hermitage, Likhita then shook down fruit that was fully ripe.
Taking them, the Brahmana ate them trustingly, and as he was eating, Shankha too came to the hermitage.
Seeing him eating, Shankha said to his brother, "Where did you get the fruit, and for what reason do you eat it?"
Bowing and touching water, he said to his elder brother, smiling as it were, "I took it from here."
Then Shankha, filled with fierce anger, said to him, "You have committed theft by taking the fruit yourself; go to the king and proclaim your deed."
Sudyumna, hearing from the border guards that Likhita had come, went on foot with his ministers, the lord of men.
Meeting him, the king said to that best of Brahma-knowers: "Tell me why you have come, revered one; it is as good as done."
Thus addressed, the Brahmin-sage said to Sudyumna: "Promise, 'I will do it'; having heard, you ought to do it.
Fruits not given by my elder have been eaten by me, bull among men; punish me for that without delay."
[Sudyumna said:] "If the king is held to be the authority in bearing the rod, then in granting permission too there should be a reason, best of Brahmanas.
You, permitted, pure in deeds and of great vows, ask for other wishes; I shall do your word."
[Vyasa said:] Though urged by the great-souled king, the Brahmin-sage chose no other boon than the rod.
Then the king cut off the hands of the great-souled Likhita, and he, having borne the rod, went away.
Going to his brother Shankha, he said in distress, "Revered one, forgive me, ill-minded one, who have borne the rod."
[Shankha said:] "I am not angry with you, knower of dharma, nor do you offend me; you transgressed dharma, and so your atonement has been made.
Go quickly to the Bahuda and duly offer libations to gods, ancestors and sages; and do not set your mind on unrighteousness."
[Vyasa said:] Hearing Shankha's words, Likhita entered the holy river and began the water-offering.
Then two hands like lotuses appeared to him; astonished, he showed those hands to his brother.
Then Shankha said to him, "This was done by me by austerity; do not doubt it; it is fate that ordains."
[Likhita said:] "Why did you not purify me before, radiant one, who have such power of austerity, best of the twice-born?"
[Shankha said:] "It had to be so done by me; I am not a bearer of the rod for you; that king is purified, and you with your ancestors."
[Vyasa said:] "That king, best of the Pandavas, was the best by that deed and attained supreme perfection like Daksha son of Prachetas.
This is the dharma of kshatriyas, the protection of subjects; in this wrong course, great king, do not set your mind on grief.
Hear the beneficial word of this brother, best of knowers of dharma: the rod, O king of kings, is the kshatriya's dharma, not shaving the head."

The wishes, dear one, of your brothers who dwelt in the forest as ascetics, Yudhishthira, which they had there,
mahabharata:12:25.3	let these great chariot-warriors obtain them, bull of the Bharatas; rule the earth, Partha, like Yayati son of Nahusha.
mahabharata:12:25.4	You, ascetics, endured a painful dwelling in the forest; at the end of sorrow, tigers among men, let these now experience happiness.
mahabharata:12:25.5	Having experienced dharma, wealth and desire with your brothers, Bharata, afterwards you may depart, lord of men.
mahabharata:12:25.6	Become quit of your debt to guests, ancestors and gods, son of Kunti, and then you shall go to heaven.
mahabharata:12:25.7	Sacrifice with the Sarvamedha and Ashvamedha, delight of the Kurus; then afterwards, great king, you will go to the supreme state.
mahabharata:12:25.8	Having joined all your brothers with sacrifices of abundant fees, you will gain unequalled fame, Pandava.
mahabharata:12:25.9	We know your word, tiger among men, delight of the Kurus; hear from me how by acting a king does not fall from dharma.
mahabharata:12:25.11	A king who shows a robber the right time and place, relying on wisdom born of the scriptures, is not touched by sin.
mahabharata:12:25.12	A king who takes a sixth share and does not protect the kingdom takes on that sin to the extent of a fourth part.
mahabharata:12:25.13	Learn how a king does not fall from dharma: restraining by the law books, following the rule, fearless, disregarding desire and anger, equal-eyed like a father.
mahabharata:12:25.14	When a king is struck by fate in the time of action, and neglects that action, they do not call it a transgression.
mahabharata:12:25.15	Enemies must be restrained, whether by force or by design; one should not make peace with sinners nor let the kingdom be sold.
mahabharata:12:25.16	Heroes and the noble and the learned are to be honoured, Yudhishthira; those with cattle and the wealthy are especially to be protected.
mahabharata:12:25.17	The learned are to be appointed in lawful affairs; and a wise man should not trust a single one, even if full of merits.
mahabharata:12:25.18	An unprotecting, ill-mannered, proud, stiff and envious king is joined to sin and is called ill-controlled.
mahabharata:12:25.19	Those who are lost when not protected, under a king struck by fate, and those killed by thieves—all that is the king's sin.
mahabharata:12:25.20	When good counsel has been taken and good policy followed, and effort duly made and the action done, there is no unrighteousness, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:25.21	Undertakings fail and also succeed by fate; but when human effort is made, sin does not touch the king.
mahabharata:12:25.22	Here I shall tell you this story, tiger among kings, of what befell the former royal sage Hayagriva, O king.
mahabharata:12:25.23	Having slain his enemies, and himself slain in the battle, the hero of untroubled deeds, alone, steadfast, conquered, Yudhishthira,
mahabharata:12:25.24	by the deed in restraining his foes and the supreme yoga in protecting his people, having done deeds and gained fame in a good fight, Hayagriva rejoices in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:12:25.25	With his self given up in battles, an attacker, cut by weapons and harassed by robbers, Ashvagriva, the great soul of fixed conduct, perfected in soul, rejoices in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:12:25.26	The bow the sacrificial post, the bowstring the girdle, the arrow the ladle, the sword the spoon, blood the ghee; the chariot the altar, battle the fire at will, the four best horses the four priests;
mahabharata:12:25.27	having offered his enemies in that sacrificial fire, freed of sin, the lion among kings, the energetic one, having offered his life at the avabhritha in battle, Hayagriva rejoices in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:12:25.28	Protecting the kingdom with design and policy, self-given, given to sacrifice, the great-souled, high-minded, pervading all worlds with his fame, Hayagriva rejoices in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:12:25.29	Having protected the earth by divine success and human policy of the rod, by the principles of yoga, the king, righteous, great-souled Hayagriva rejoices in heaven.
mahabharata:12:25.30	The learned, renouncing, faithful, grateful, having left the human world and done his deed, the king ascended to the world of the wise and learned and esteemed who gave up their bodies.
mahabharata:12:25.31	Having rightly obtained the Vedas and studied the scriptures, rightly protected the kingdom, the great soul, having established the four classes in their own dharma, Hayagriva rejoices in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:12:25.32	Having won battles and protected subjects, drunk soma and satisfied the best of the twice-born, having borne the rod rightly for his people, exhausted in battle he rejoices in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:12:25.33	He whose conduct men praise and whom the good and learned honour as worthy, having conquered heaven and gone to the worlds of heroes, the great soul of holy fame attained perfection.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Neither this kingdom of the earth nor the various pleasures please my mind today; this grief makes me roar.
And hearing the lament of the women bereft of heroes and sons, sage, I find no peace."
Thus addressed, Vyasa, best of those who know yoga, knower of dharma, versed in the Veda, replied to the greatly wise Yudhishthira:

It is not gained by action or by thought, nor does anyone give it to man; by the turn of Time as ordained by the Creator, a man gets everything in time.
mahabharata:12:26.6	Not by wisdom or study of scriptures can distinctions be won by men out of time; even a fool sometimes gains aims; for Time is without distinction regarding any deed.
mahabharata:12:26.7	Out of time neither craft nor mantras nor herbs give their fruit; when gathered by Time, they succeed and flourish in due time.
mahabharata:12:26.8	By Time swift winds blow; by Time rain comes from the clouds; by Time water is full of lotuses and blue lotuses; by Time trees flower in forests.
mahabharata:12:26.9	By Time nights are dark and bright; by Time the moon is full-orbed; out of time trees give no flower or fruit; out of time rivers do not flow with force.
mahabharata:12:26.11	Out of time none dies or is born; out of time a child does not speak; out of time youth does not come; out of time a sown seed does not sprout.
mahabharata:12:26.12	Out of time the sun does not come to its conjunction; out of time it does not go to the western mountain; out of time the moon and the ocean with their great waves neither wax nor wane.
mahabharata:12:26.13	Here too they tell this ancient history, sung by King Senajit, afflicted with grief, Yudhishthira:
mahabharata:12:26.14	This cycle touches all mortals, hard to cross; all men, ripened by Time, die.
mahabharata:12:26.15	Men kill others, O king, and others kill them too; this is the worldly term: neither does one kill nor is one killed.
mahabharata:12:26.16	Some think 'He kills,' others 'He does not kill'; but the arising and passing of beings are fixed by nature.
mahabharata:12:26.17	When wealth, a wife, a son or a father is lost or dead, one should deal with grief thinking 'Alas, how painful!'
mahabharata:12:26.18	Why do you grieve, being a fool? What is there to grieve for? Look at sorrows within sorrows and fears within fears.
mahabharata:12:26.19	Even this self is not mine, nor is the whole earth mine; seeing that as it is mine so it is others', one is not bewildered.
mahabharata:12:26.20	Thousands of occasions of grief and hundreds of occasions of joy enter the fool day after day, not the wise man.
mahabharata:12:26.21	Thus by Time these pleasant and unpleasant things, sorrows and joys, turn in portions among living beings.
mahabharata:12:26.22	There is only sorrow, no joy; therefore it is found; sorrow is born of craving's pain, and joy is born of sorrow's pain.
mahabharata:12:26.23	After joy comes sorrow, after sorrow joy; one does not always get sorrow nor always joy.
mahabharata:12:26.24	Joy is at the end of sorrows and sorrow at the end of joy; therefore he who wishes eternal happiness should give up both.
mahabharata:12:26.25	That which would be the cause of grief or anguish, or confusion in sorrow, or whose root is iron—one should abandon it, even a limb.
mahabharata:12:26.26	Whether happiness or sorrow, pleasant or unpleasant, one should accept what comes, unconquered in heart.
mahabharata:12:26.27	When a little unpleasantness comes even from one's limbs, wives or sons, then you will know who is whose, by what and how.
mahabharata:12:26.28	Those who are the most foolish in the world and those who have gone beyond wisdom prosper in happiness; the middle is joined to affliction.'
mahabharata:12:26.29	Thus spoke the greatly wise Senajit, Yudhishthira, knower of the high and low, of the world's dharma, of joy and sorrow.
mahabharata:12:26.30	One happy at another's sorrow can never be happy; there is no end to sorrows, for one arises after another.
mahabharata:12:26.31	Happiness and sorrow, existence and non-existence, gain and loss, death and life—all touch men in turn here; therefore the steadfast one should neither rejoice nor be angry.
mahabharata:12:26.32	Initiation in sacrifice, protection, war, yoga in the kingdom with proper policy of the rod, giving up wealth as fees in sacrifice, and right knowledge: know these as purifying.
mahabharata:12:26.33	Protecting the kingdom with design and policy, self-given, given to sacrifice, the great soul, moving in all worlds in the form of dharma, rejoices in the world of the gods after the body.
mahabharata:12:26.34	Having won battles and protected the kingdom, drunk soma and increased the subjects, having borne the rod rightly for his people, exhausted in battle he rejoices in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:12:26.35	Having rightly obtained the Vedas and studied the scriptures, and the king having rightly protected the kingdom, having established the four classes in their own dharma, he, pure in soul, rejoices in the world of the gods.
mahabharata:12:26.36	The king whose conduct men honour even when he has gone to heaven, as do townsfolk, countryfolk and ministers, is the best of kings.
[Yudhishthira said:] "In Vasushena (Karna) and the knower of dharma Dhrishtaketu, and in other kings of various lands at the meeting,
grief does not leave me, a slayer of kin, afflicted, greedy for kingdom, exceedingly fierce, the destroyer of my own family.
He on whose lap I played and rolled about—that son of Ganga was felled by me, greedy for kingdom.
When I saw him reeling, Partha, trembling from arrows as if from thunderbolts, looking at Shikhandin,
the tall lion among men, the grandsire, like an old lion, strewn with sharp arrows, my mind was pained.
When he turned away, sinking, and fell from his chariot by arrows, reeling like a mountain, I was faint.
He who with bow and arrow in hand fought Bhargava (Parashurama) for many days in the great battle at Kurukshetra,
who, the son of the river, the hero, with a single chariot challenged the assembled kshatriya kings at Varanasi for the sake of the maidens,
When I saw him fallen on the ground, drenched in blood, then a most fierce fever entered me, best of sages—he by whom we were raised as children and protected.
He was slain by me, greedy for kingdom, sinful, a slayer of my teacher, a fool, for the sake of a kingdom of short duration.
And the teacher, the great archer honoured by all kings, was falsely told by me, sinful, in the battle concerning his son.
That burns my limbs: what the teacher said to me—'You are truthful, king; if my son lives, tell me the truth'—the Brahmana asked me that, not suspecting the truth.
With an elephant as intermediary, it was falsely done by me, greedy for kingdom, sinful, a slayer of my teacher.
Putting on the cloak of truth, I said to the teacher in battle, 'Ashvatthaman is slain,' when the elephant was felled; what worlds shall I go to, having done that dreadful deed?
And that I had Karna, who never fled in battle, my fierce elder brother, killed—who is a worse sinner than I?
And that I greedily sent the boy Abhimanyu, born like a lion on the mountains, into the army protected by Drona.
Since then I cannot look at Bibhatsu or at lotus-eyed Krishna, like a guilty slayer of an embryo.
And I grieve for Draupadi, undeserving of sorrow, bereft of five sons, as the earth would be bereft of five mountains.
I, the doer of the fault, sinful, destroyer of the earth, will sit just so and dry up this body.
Know me today as sitting to fast to death, a slayer of my teacher, so that in other births I may not be the ender of a family.
I shall not eat nor drink water in any way; I shall dry up my dear life here, ascetic.
Go as you please; I give leave, having appeased you; all of you give me leave; I shall give up this body."
[Vaishampayana said:] To Partha speaking thus, distraught with grief for his kin, Vyasa, best of sages, restraining him, said, "Not so."

You should not grieve beyond measure, great king; I shall say it again: this is fated, lord.
mahabharata:12:27.28	Unions and separations of born beings are certain; like bubbles in water they come to be and cease to be.
mahabharata:12:27.29	All accumulations end in exhaustion, all risings end in falling, all unions end in separation, and life ends in death.
mahabharata:12:27.30	Happiness ends in sorrow; idleness, skill, sorrow, with happiness arising; prosperity, beauty, modesty, steadiness and success do not dwell in the unskilled.
mahabharata:12:27.31	Friends are not enough for happiness, nor enemies for sorrow; wisdom is not enough for wealth, nor wealth for happiness.
mahabharata:12:27.32	As you were created by the Creator, son of Kunti, so act in deeds; thence is your success, you are not master of yourself, O king.
[Vyasa said:] "Here too they tell this ancient history, the song of Ashma, tiger among men; hear it, Yudhishthira.
The king Janaka of Videha, flooded with grief and sorrow, questioned the wise Brahmana Ashma about a doubt.
[Janaka said:] In the gain or loss of kinsmen and of wealth, how should a man act who wishes the good?
[Ashma said:] When this self has been born to man, thereafter sorrows and joys come upon him one after another.
In the onset of either of them, whatever he resorts to, it carries off his consciousness as wind a cloud.
I am well born, I am perfected, I am not merely human—for these three reasons his mind becomes drenched.
With his mind so drenched, he abandons the enjoyments gathered by his fathers and, wasted, thinks taking others' property good.
Kings, greedy, forbid him, who has transgressed bounds and is taking what is not his, as they do a deer with arrows.
Men who are twenty or thirty years old will not exist after a hundred years, king.
For those greatest sorrows, one should prescribe the remedy by wisdom, looking at the conduct of all living beings here and there.
The source of mental sorrows is confusion of mind or the onset of the unwanted; a third does not obtain.
Thus these and those sorrows, various, and those of touch, come upon man here.
Old age and death devour beings like two wolves, the strong and the weak, the small and the great.
No man ever passes beyond old age and death, even having conquered this earth to the ocean's edge.
Happiness or sorrow come upon beings and must be obtained helplessly; there is no avoiding it.
In youth, middle age or the last age, O king, those things are unavoidable and what is desired turns out otherwise.
Separation from the very dear and union with the unloved, gain and loss, happiness and sorrow, follow the ordinance.
The appearance of beings, the laying down of the body, the attainment and exertion—all this is fixed.
Scent, colour, taste and touch cease by nature; so do happiness and sorrow follow the ordinance.
Sitting, lying, going, rising, drinking and eating of all beings are fixed and come only by Time.
Physicians too are sick, the strong are very weak, those with wives are impotent; strange is the turn of Time.
Birth in a family, valour, health, steadiness, good fortune and enjoyment are gained by what is to be.
The poor who do not wish for them have very many sons; the many who wish for them have none; the prosperous striving do not.
Disease, fire, water, weapon, hunger, wild beast, poison, death by rope, and a fall from a height—
whatever a man's departure is fated to be, he goes by that cause; none is seen to evade it, nor has any escaped it.
A rich man is seen to perish while young, and a poor, afflicted man lives a hundred years, O lord of men.
Men without possessions are seen to live long, and those born in prosperous families perish like moths.
Mostly the fortunate in this world lack the power to enjoy, while even wood is digested by the poor, O king.
Driven by Time, one thinks "I do this," and the ill-natured, from discontent, does whatever sin he desires.
Women, dice, hunting and drink are censured by the wise for their attachment, yet many learned men are seen attached to them.
Thus by Time all desired and undesired things touch all beings; no cause is found.
Wind, sky, fire, moon and sun, day and night, luminaries, rivers and mountains—who makes or sustains them?
Cold, heat and rain turn by Time; so too the happiness and sorrow of men, bull among men.
Neither herbs nor scriptures nor oblations nor prayers save a man seized by death or old age.
As two logs meet in the great ocean, meet and part, so is the meeting of beings.
Those who are attended by men and women with song and music, and the helpless who eat others' food—Time acts equally on them.
Thousands of mothers and fathers and hundreds of sons and wives have been experienced in cycles of existence—whose are they, or whose are we?
No one will be anyone's, and this one is no one's; this is a meeting on the road with wives, kinsmen and companions.

Where did I dwell, where shall I go, who am I, why am I here, from what and for whom should I grieve?—so should one settle the mind in this impermanent, dear companionship, in the cycle of existence moving like a wheel."
If the fault lies in Time, and if even there it is not accepted, then the fault is not to be tested by me, for we are not authorised here.
The earth was destroyed by Duryodhana for the sake of wealth, and the treasury of the ill-minded son of Dhritarashtra too is ruined.
Then Bhima, in the midst of friends, made the sound of slapping his arms, intolerant, in the hearing of Dhritarashtra and Gandhari.
Then those great chariot-warriors of the Vrishnis and Andhakas, wishing to go, with their households, bulls among men, desired a pilgrimage.
Thus addressed by Bhimasena, Yudhishthira, righteous, best of the wise, replied about Nakula:
But Yudhishthira, disheartened, overcome by that stench, was resolved to turn back and turned around, Bharata.
